proposals.butler: where the waves had raised a high beach of shingle
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, unsure): “a beach of pebbles”; note: “British usage; many readers think of roof shingles”.
proposals.reason: Beach shingle (rounded pebbles) is British usage. For American readers, and the edition is in American English, a ‘shingle’ is a roofing tile or a signboard, and ‘a beach of shingle’ cannot be pictured. Homer’s point is the pebbles the sea washes up (6.94–95), on which the clean laundry is spread. ‘pebbles’ is plain English on both sides of the Atlantic and adds nothing. Unlike the case for keeping ‘draughts’ (GLOSSARY), the replacement is not a regionalism. D29 would keep ‘shingle’ if the lead judges it current enough for the edition’s readers, which is why this is optional.

proposals.quote_modern: for he was in great want
proposals.replacement: for he was in great need
proposals.butler: as he drew near to them all naked as he was, for he was in great want
proposals.reader_evidence: The reader flagged “archaic ‘Even such’ and ‘in great want’” (pause) and read it correctly: “‘for he was in great want’ means need drove him to approach them naked”. The book-level notes list ‘in great want’ among the old-fashioned forms.
proposals.reason: ‘want’ meaning need is one of the brief’s dead senses, and here the living sense is a hazard. A naked man approaching young women ‘for he was in great want’ can be read as desire, which inverts his motive and the decorum of the scene. Homer: ‘for need had come upon him’ (6.136). ‘need’ fixes the sense with one word. The living idioms ‘for want of a foothold’ (5.30) and ‘you shall not want for clothes’ (6.14) are not affected and are kept. It is optional because most readers take ‘in want’ as need, as this reader did.

proposals.quote_modern: in the middle of it, paved with large stones
proposals.replacement: in the middle of it, and paved with large stones
proposals.butler: You will see the market place with a temple of Neptune in the middle of it, and paved with large stones bedded in the earth.
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (syntax, pause): “The marketplace (probably not the temple) is paved with large stones set into the ground”. The reader was only moderately confident.
proposals.reason: The candidate dropped Butler’s ‘and’, which leaves ‘paved with large stones’ attached to the nearest noun, the temple, so the reader had to guess which of the two is paved. In Homer the paved space is the assembly place around the temple (6.266–267). Restoring Butler’s own ‘and’ (D29) makes ‘paved’ a second predicate of the marketplace, and no other word moves.
proposals.collision_check: This restores Butler’s own word and introduces no new one.

rejected_barriers.quote: near the lawless Cyclopes
rejected_barriers.reason: The Cyclopes are named here and told of in Book 9. This is not a wording problem.

rejected_barriers.quote: But he was dead and gone to the house of Hades
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. Butler does not say here whether Alcinous is Nausithous’s son either.

rejected_barriers.quote: the famous sea captain Dymas’s daughter
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s word order, read correctly: ‘famous’ modifies Dymas, as in Homer 6.22. A pause, not a misreading.

rejected_barriers.quote: coming up to the girl’s bedside like a breath of wind, she hovered over her head
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s narrative order. The dream is revealed at ¶4 in the source as well.

rejected_barriers.quote: you are going to be married almost immediately
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s wording (Homer: ‘your marriage is near’). The reader’s inference is correct.

rejected_barriers.quote: should find good clothes for those who attend you
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s wording (Homer means the bridal party). The reader’s reading is acceptable, and the vagueness is the source’s.

rejected_barriers.quote: the washing cisterns
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s object, decoded (‘washing pools or tanks’). ¶8 shows water running through them.

rejected_barriers.quote: to tell her father and mother all about it
rejected_barriers.reason: A narrative observation, not a wording issue.

rejected_barriers.quote: a good strong wagon with a body to it
rejected_barriers.reason: Decoded correctly (‘a box or bed’). Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: so that she and her women could anoint themselves
rejected_barriers.reason: A custom, decoded correctly, and ‘anoint’ is current.

rejected_barriers.quote: vied with one another in treading them in the pits
rejected_barriers.reason: A custom, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Then they had their dinner
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly as the midday meal: the same passage says they waited for the sun to dry the clothes. ‘dinner’ for the main meal is current in many regions, and the edition keeps it throughout (the candidates for Books 3, 4, 9, 10 and 24).

rejected_barriers.quote: daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus
rejected_barriers.reason: The glossary row keeps ‘aegis’ unglossed (Book 3 table; Book 5 and 6 table).

rejected_barriers.quote: Leto is proud then to see her daughter
rejected_barriers.reason: Inferable from ‘her daughter’, as the reader inferred it. Butler’s wording (the glossary keeps Leto).

rejected_barriers.quote: At any rate I am among a race of men and women
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s wording, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Even such did Odysseus seem to the young women
rejected_barriers.reason: ‘Even such’ is old but not a false friend, because no modern idiom competes with it, and it was read correctly (‘as frightening and desperate as the lion’). The lion simile’s present tense is Butler’s. The same note’s ‘in great want’ is proposal B06-02.

rejected_barriers.quote: scampered off along the spits that jutted out into the sea
rejected_barriers.reason: Decoded correctly, and the relative clause explains it.

rejected_barriers.quote: embrace her knees as a suppliant
rejected_barriers.reason: Supplication is the poem’s custom. The text shows Odysseus’s choice and its risk, and a gloss would add interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: O queen
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s (Homer’s ἄνασσα), read correctly as a flattering form of address.

rejected_barriers.quote: the man whose wedding gifts have been the richest
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s wording, read correctly as bride-gifts. ‘richest’ and ‘takes you to his own home’ carry the custom.

rejected_barriers.quote: on the journey that has been the source of all my troubles
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s reference to the Trojan expedition. It needs outside knowledge only.

rejected_barriers.quote: the Ogygian island
rejected_barriers.reason: Ogygia is named in Book 1 (glossary). Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: let me have anything you may have brought here to wrap your clothes in
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: and they themselves know more about it than anyone
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s rendering of an ambiguous Homeric phrase (6.185), and both of the reader’s readings are live. Resolving it would add interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: you appear to be a sensible, well-disposed person. There is no accounting for luck.
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly, and ‘no accounting for’ is a current idiom.

rejected_barriers.quote: a land’s end that juts into the sounding sea
rejected_barriers.reason: An epithet, decoded correctly. Kept.

rejected_barriers.quote: They will take what they can get and be thankful
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s wording, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s image, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: as a skillful workman enriches a piece of silver plate by gilding it
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. The candidate has already placed the Hephaestus clause after the noun it modifies.

rejected_barriers.quote: I should like my future husband to be just such a man as he is, if only he would stay here
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. Her hint is in the source.

rejected_barriers.quote: Meanwhile Nausicaa thought of another matter
rejected_barriers.reason: The glossary formula (Book 5 and 6 table: ‘bethought her of another matter’ → ‘thought of another matter’). Read well enough.

rejected_barriers.quote: I will introduce you at the house of my excellent father
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s word. The tension the reader notices, that she will ‘introduce’ him and then sends him in alone (¶22), is in Butler, since Homer’s verb means ‘send or escort’. The reader understood the plan, and this is not the edition’s to fix.

rejected_barriers.quote: a good harbor on either side with a narrow entrance into the city
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s layout (Homer 6.262–264). A difficulty in picturing it, not a wording problem.

rejected_barriers.quote: the ships drawn up along the roadside
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: for we have no neighbors
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: It would be a good thing if she would take herself off and find a husband somewhere else
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s sarcasm inside the imagined gossip, read correctly, and ‘take herself off’ is current.

rejected_barriers.quote: while her father and mother were still alive
rejected_barriers.reason: The poem’s cultural logic. Nothing in the wording hides it.

rejected_barriers.quote: without having been married in the face of all the world
rejected_barriers.reason: Recoverable, and read correctly (‘publicly’).

rejected_barriers.quote: give you an escort
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: one of the bearing-posts
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept by the earlier decision (continuity §5, B06-P023), and read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Never mind him, but go up to my mother, and lay your hands on her knees
rejected_barriers.reason: The poem’s custom, not a wording problem.

rejected_barriers.quote: daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, unwearying
rejected_barriers.reason: The prayer formula fixed by the glossary (B04-P068), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: for you paid no heed to my prayers when Poseidon was wrecking me
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s and Homer’s complaint (6.325). The tension with Book 5 is the poem’s and is not to be fixed.

rejected_barriers.quote: she was afraid of her uncle Poseidon
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. Poseidon’s motive belongs to Books 1 and 9.

reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.reader_said: He has never seen such beauty, except a young palm tree he once admired beside Apollo’s altar at Delos
reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.butler: I can only compare you to a young palm tree which I saw when I was at Delos growing near the altar of Apollo
reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.why_text_is_clear: The candidate says ‘I can only compare you to a young palm tree…’, which is a comparison and not an exception. The reader’s ‘except’ compresses it harmlessly; nothing to repair.

recurring.rendering: ‘in great want’ → ‘in great need’ (6.11). The living idioms ‘for want of’ (5.30) and ‘not want for’ (6.14) are kept
kept, with no change, as in the candidates for Books 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 23 and 24

kept, with no change. For the record, not for repair: 6.8 prints ‘So did the girl outshine her handmaids’ where 5.31 and 5.36 print ‘even so did’, two renderings of one Butler formula across the two Books, neither of them a comprehension problem

summary: Book 6 reads mostly as modern prose. The reader’s paraphrase is correct in all 26 paragraphs, and the rest of the 46 barriers concern customs the poem shows without explaining (supplication, anointing, bride-gifts, washing clothes by treading), names and references from earlier Books, or tensions that are Butler’s own (Nausicaa ‘introduces’ Odysseus and then sends him in alone; Odysseus says Athena ignored his prayers). There is no blocking or recommended problem. There are three optional repairs: ‘in great want’ (a naked man approaching young women, where ‘want’ can read as desire; Homer says ‘need’), ‘a high beach of shingle’ (roofing to American readers; ‘pebbles’), and Butler’s own ‘and’ restored at ¶20 so that the marketplace, not the temple, is paved. The sweep found nothing further. ‘presently’, ‘dinner’, ‘Even such’, ‘bearing-posts’, the prayer formula and ‘thought of another matter’ are kept, by edition-wide usage or by glossary rule. Paragraph numbers are 0-based, as in the pairs files.
